spec.topic: Should schools replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences?

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Tonight we are discussing whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Annelise, you support the change.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Twice-yearly conferences let teachers discuss a student's progress in detail, which is why the replacement is worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My daughter has attended the same school since kindergarten. I am not convinced that a meeting can replace something families can read at home.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some teachers already spend their evenings preparing detailed comments for families. The new system would give families specific next steps, because a conversation can turn those comments into an actionable plan.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Those specific next steps would make it easier for families to support learning between meetings. That is why conferences could lead to more useful follow-up than a report card alone.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Maeve, what is your strongest objection to replacing the reports?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later. Because that record remains available after a meeting, schools should retain a written reporting system alongside any conferences.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So Annelise is proposing that schools use two parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards. Maeve, do you think the written record is essential?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, Maeve is saying that report cards offer parents a lasting written record. We will leave the audience to weigh that concern against the proposed follow-up benefits.

spec.topic: Should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses?

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses? Jelena, you start us off.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Every household should keep a shared emergency cash fund, because repair bills and other unexpected costs arrive without any warning.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: A fund also spares families from borrowing at high interest, which is another reason to have one.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: But a fund tempts people to dip into it for holidays and gadgets, so it rarely stays intact.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: So, Jelena, in other words you are saying every household needs a pot of cash set aside together for emergencies?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Exactly. Our own fund began after a flooded kitchen in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Clement, where should such a fund be kept?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: It should sit in an easily accessible account rather than in a drawer at home, since cash kept at home can be stolen.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: And cash in a drawer earns no interest, which is a further reason for an account.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: I will grant that point, because insurers often do not cover cash that is stolen or burnt at home.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: My sister works as a financial adviser, by the way.

spec.topic: Should annual bonuses depend more on team performance than individual targets?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets. Laleh, make the case for a stronger team component.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team performance should carry more weight than individual targets in determining annual bonuses. Most important work is interdependent.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Individual targets reveal each employee's accountability. A bonus system should show who delivered what.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Because work is interdependent, a team-weighted bonus would encourage employees to help colleagues meet shared deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team-based bonuses would reward cooperation between departments, since departments often succeed or fail together.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: A team-weighted bonus would reduce rivalry between employees competing for individual results. That is another reason to give team performance greater weight.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team performance gives a better measure of success when employees depend on one another's work, which is why it belongs at the centre of the bonus calculation.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Individual targets make responsibility for results visible. That matters because managers need to know who is accountable.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Individual targets allow managers to identify employees who need coaching, so they should not be pushed into the background.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Since individual targets also keep responsibility for results visible, they remain valuable even when the bonus includes a team element.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: But individual targets can encourage employees to ignore team priorities. That is why I reject making them the dominant basis for bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: So you are saying that individual targets reveal who is accountable?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Exactly, although individual targets can pull employees away from shared priorities. In other words, they can make personal achievement compete with teamwork.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: The company introduced its current bonus scheme six years ago. We should judge the proposed change on its effects, not its age.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: The finance department publishes the bonus figures every January. That schedule will not change under either model.

spec.topic: Should publicly funded research be required to publish all results, including failed experiments?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments, because taxpayers pay for every experiment, whether it succeeds or fails.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Negative results are routinely left in drawers, and that is why other laboratories repeat experiments that have already failed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Repeating known failures wastes public money, which is the strongest reason to change the rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say researchers will not have time to write up every failed experiment, which makes mandatory publication unworkable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a short structured note of a few paragraphs takes an afternoon to write, so the writing burden is small.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Journals already reject dull papers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Open repositories can host failed results without any journal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Failed experiments can only be understood when the full method is shared. In other words, shared methods let others judge why an experiment failed.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I spent a year in a chemistry lab.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Publishing everything gives the public the whole record of what was funded.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, requiring publication of everything would make the public record of funded work complete.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Funding bodies could enforce the rule by withholding the final grant payment until results are deposited.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, science is a conversation in which every result, good or bad, is a contribution, and the rule that all results be published simply says so.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I spent two years as a laboratory technician.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Researchers fear that negative results will damage their careers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, funders could count published negative results in grant assessments, which would remove that fear.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Medical trials are where hidden failures do the most harm to patients, since patients can be given treatments whose earlier failures were never disclosed.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes, I support that requirement because a minority juror can identify overlooked evidence or reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You have thought about the issue carefully. What makes unanimity important?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I have never served on a jury.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I also prefer written questions to live interview questions.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: That requirement matters because unanimous verdicts make jurors take reasonable doubt seriously.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest objection to your position?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But a single juror can block a verdict despite very strong evidence. That danger is why serious criminal trials should allow a retrial after a jury deadlock.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that a deadlock should lead to a retrial rather than an immediate conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Exactly. A single dissent can force a serious criminal trial to be repeated, and because of that every serious-offence trial needs a clear procedure for dealing with a deadlocked jury.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you think unanimous verdicts need a defined deadlock procedure.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes. Several comparable legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts; this comparison shows that unanimity is not the only possible way to protect fairness in serious criminal trials.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So your comparative point is that qualified-majority systems provide an alternative to unanimous verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Before we finish, is there anything personal you want to add?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I keep a copy of the jury handbook on my desk.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, you think internal advertising can create a costly delay in filling a position.

utterances.text: Managers can set a five-day window for internal applications. Because that window is short, it need not create a long hiring delay.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal advertising makes the promotion process more transparent.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Employees trust promotion decisions more when opportunities are visible, so transparency has a practical benefit.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that visible opportunities make employees more trusting of promotion decisions.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal advertising gives employees a fair chance to apply, which is another reason managers should follow the requirement.

spec.topic: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Planning rules should require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system, since households use treated drinking-quality water for flushing toilets and watering gardens, which do not need it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a second reason: roof run-off captured at the source reduces the load on storm drains during heavy downpours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Builders will say that a rainwater tank costs far too much to include in every home.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a basic tank and pipework add under one percent to the build cost of a typical new house, which is why I reject the objection about cost.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A blanket requirement would also be simple to enforce, because a single standard leaves builders no room to argue over exemptions.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Esther, should banks be allowed to replace passwords with facial recognition?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, they should be allowed to use facial recognition instead of passwords, because passwords are routinely reused, phished and stolen.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some people worry that a leaked face cannot be reset the way a password can.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: That ignores how it works: banks store encrypted mathematical templates rather than photographs, so a breach would not expose usable images of anyone's face.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the stored data would be useless to thieves.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Logging in by face takes about a second, which is another reason to allow it. Incidentally, I have used it on my own banking app for two years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about customers whose faces the system misreads, or who cannot use it at all?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Banks must keep a fallback such as a PIN for those customers, since some systems have higher error rates for darker skin tones.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, customers must be able to opt out.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly, banks should make face login optional, because data protection law requires customer consent for biometric processing.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would all this be expensive to roll out?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Rollout would cost banks only a modest amount, since customers' phones already contain suitable cameras.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Esther

spec.topic: Should youth football leagues prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should youth football leagues prohibit heading until players reach sixteen? Dolores, you support the motion.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen because repeated heading can cause cumulative effects from minor impacts.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A blanket prohibition on heading is unnecessary because trained coaches can teach safe heading technique without allowing heading in matches.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Players under sixteen need gradual preparation before they can head the ball safely, and gradual preparation can be provided through soft balls and controlled drills.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: A complete ban would prevent coaches from identifying players who need extra help with heading technique, since regular supervised practice helps coaches identify those players.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Karima, does your alternative allow any heading in competitive matches?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: The regional youth league introduced new concussion forms this season. That administrative change does not settle the question before us.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Youth leagues can permit carefully supervised heading before players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, a blanket prohibition on heading is unnecessary. That is my objection to the proposed ban, and that is why youth leagues can permit carefully supervised heading before players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: The under-fourteen championship has twelve teams registered. We will now hear closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate: should youth football leagues prohibit heading until players reach sixteen? Isaac supports the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Repeated heading can expose young players to lasting brain injury, because a review by paediatric neurologists found evidence of repeated heading impacts in young players.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Dolores, you oppose a complete prohibition?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: I do. That evidence is why youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: The regional youth final will be played on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: So you are saying that the paediatric neurologists' review found evidence of repeated heading impacts in young players.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Karima, what alternative protection would you put in place?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Since those findings concern possible harm, youth football leagues should introduce strict medical monitoring for heading-related symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Heading is a technical skill that can be taught progressively.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, heading is a teachable technical skill. Because it is teachable, coaches can teach players a safer heading technique before the players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: But young players cannot reliably apply a safe heading technique under match pressure, so that argument does not justify allowing heading.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Florin, what is your strongest objection to the proposed age limit?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Since heading is an important part of older football, removing heading until sixteen would leave players unprepared for the demands of older football.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: I volunteer at a girls' football club on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now take closing statements from each panellist.

spec.topic: Should secondary schools require every student to complete a financial-literacy course before graduating?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should every secondary school student have to pass a financial-literacy course before graduating?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Yes, every student should complete one before graduating, because too many young adults take on debt they do not understand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why do they not understand it?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Loan and credit card contracts use terms that most eighteen-year-olds were never taught, and that is why they borrow blindly. Another reason to require the course is that it gives every student the same grounding whatever their family income.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that the course would put students from poorer and richer families on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Exactly. My sister learned about budgeting only after her first overdraft.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Teachers say the timetable is already crowded.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Some say the timetable is too full for another required course, but the course needs only about thirty hours in total.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And who would teach it?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Existing maths teachers can deliver it with modest training, since the core material is percentages and compound interest. That is one more reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, no specialists would need to be hired.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Right. In states that already require the course, graduates open savings accounts more often, which shows the course changes behaviour, and that is why schools should make it compulsory.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Only that I teach evening classes at a community college.

spec.topic: Should voting be compulsory, with a modest penalty for eligible citizens who abstain without justification?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Item two is compulsory voting with a modest fine. Kai, would you start?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: I think voting should be compulsory, with a modest fine for unjustified abstention, because turnout in our local elections is below forty percent.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Where does that figure come from?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: I say that because the electoral commission counted thirty-seven percent at the last local election.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: But a fine would fall hardest on low-income citizens, since they have the least slack to absorb it.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So you are saying people on low incomes would be punished for being poor.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Yes. My cousin stood in a ward election last year, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Voluntary turnout shows which citizens genuinely care about the outcome.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So you are saying elections should be decided only by the keenest voters.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Partly, because forced votes are often arbitrary: disengaged people tick boxes at random.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: A note: the room is booked only until four o'clock. Kai, what size of fine do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Around ten pounds, because the commission's consultation suggested that figure.

spec.topic: Should public transport authorities use facial recognition to identify fare evaders?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether public transport authorities should use facial recognition to identify fare evaders. Priya, make the case for it.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Facial recognition can compare passenger faces with records of known fare evaders in seconds.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Because the system compares faces in seconds, inspectors could flag suspected fare evaders before they leave a station. That early flag matters because facial recognition would help authorities reduce repeat fare evasion.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: But facial recognition can misidentify innocent passengers, which is an objection to relying on it to reduce repeat evasion. The reason is that facial-recognition error rates can differ sharply between demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The transport authority's current procurement contract expires in June.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Before we move on, the busiest station has twelve platforms. Priya, how would you answer the privacy concern?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: A facial-recognition pilot at two stations would limit the number of images collected. Therefore, a facial-recognition pilot at two stations would reduce privacy exposure.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So you are saying that a two-station facial-recognition pilot would reduce privacy exposure.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: In other words, my concern is that facial recognition could wrongly penalize innocent passengers.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: You have both identified benefits and safeguards. What conclusion should viewers take from that?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Because facial recognition could help reduce repeat fare evasion, and because a limited pilot would reduce privacy exposure, public transport authorities should use facial recognition in a tightly limited pilot with strict deletion rules and human review.

spec.topic: Should governments restore wetlands even when doing so removes land from potential housing development?

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments restore wetlands even when that costs us potential housing land? Aiko, you start.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Yes, they should restore them. Wetlands absorb floodwater that would otherwise reach nearby homes, which is why I back restoration.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Theo, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Restoring wetlands is not worth losing housing land. Though flood damage to homes costs the country more each year than the housing could provide, I wonder if that is true here.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Astrid, your view?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: The country has a severe housing shortage, with young families priced out of towns. That is why wetland restoration worsens the problem, and so it is not worth the land.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: So, Aiko, you are saying that wetlands protect existing homes and so deserve priority over new building?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Exactly, put another way, wetlands protect existing homes better than new building does.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Most of the land earmarked for housing in the region is former farmland, not wetland.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I grew up beside a marsh, so this matters to me.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Wetland restoration does not have to compete with housing, because brownfield sites can be built on instead, and that is a reason to restore them.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: The last wetland scheme finished two years late. We will see what the audience thinks after the break.

spec.topic: Should businesses replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should businesses replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: They should consider it because unlimited paid leave can reduce the administrative work involved in tracking holiday balances.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: It can also help employees take time off when they genuinely need it.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: A fixed allowance sometimes encourages employees to use unnecessary days before the allowance expires.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Unlimited paid leave may also make a business seem more attractive to potential recruits.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: For those reasons, businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But unlimited paid leave can encourage employees to take less holiday because they fear appearing uncommitted.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: That concern is important. What safeguards would you introduce?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that businesses should abandon fixed holiday allowances and let employees take paid leave without a preset limit?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, replacing a fixed holiday allowance means giving employees paid leave without a preset annual limit.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You began working in human resources eight years ago, correct?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Yes, and I prefer conducting interviews in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: The district has eighteen secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Amir, what policy would you put to the schools?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Schools should abolish class rankings. The question is whether competition is helping students learn.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: The reason I support abolition is that class rankings make students focus on their position rather than on learning. Abolishing them would also let teachers emphasize individual improvement.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I disagree with abolishing rankings altogether, because class rankings provide students with useful feedback about their performance.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Public rank lists make students compare social status. Because students then compare status instead of progress, comparing social status increases anxiety among students; that is why schools should abolish class rankings.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should abolish class rankings.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I was ranked fourth in my graduating class, and that experience shaped how I think about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Schools should retain private progress reports because private progress reports identify the subjects in which each student needs help.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: That is another reason to replace public rankings: private progress reports give useful feedback without creating a public ladder of status.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: In other words, schools should keep feedback private rather than publish a ranking.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: One more reason to abolish rankings is that doing so would allow schools to recognize cooperation instead of competition.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Put another way, schools should use private progress reports as their feedback system.

spec.topic: Should election day become a public holiday?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Election day should become a public holiday. I support that because many hourly workers cannot vote during a standard workday.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because many hourly workers cannot vote during a standard workday, a public holiday would give them time to vote. As an aside, my train was delayed that morning.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: But a public holiday would not necessarily increase voter turnout. Several countries with holiday elections still have uneven turnout, which is why I am skeptical.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A public holiday would standardize voting leave across employers. Employers would not need separate voting-leave arrangements because the day would already be recognized nationally.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Public holidays can reduce the availability of some essential services. Hospitals and care homes would still need to be staffed on election day, since they cannot simply close.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: An election-day holiday would require some essential services to operate, and that is an objection to making the day a holiday. Hospitals and care homes cannot close for a public holiday, which is why staffing would remain necessary.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So Marisol is saying that a public holiday would give workers a reliable opportunity to vote.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Exactly; in other words, election day would be a day when workers could be free to vote.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: To put Bernard's proposal another way, election day would be treated like a national day off.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: What Annelise means is that a holiday might not by itself raise voter turnout.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I would also prefer voting booths to use paper ballots, though that is a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: A national election holiday would make election dates easier to remember. Equal access to voting is a legitimate public goal.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Because a holiday would give workers time to vote, standardize leave, and make the date easier to remember—and because equal access is a legitimate public goal—Parliament should make election day a public holiday.

spec.topic: Should councils allow residents to vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Our question is whether councils should let residents decide directly how a fixed share of the annual budget is spent. Dolores, you support the idea.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: A fixed portion of the annual budget would limit the scope of residents' decisions; because of that safeguard, councils should let residents vote directly on how that portion is spent.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: For that same reason, a limited vote would give residents meaningful influence without handing them control of the whole budget.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Gabriela, what protects essential services under this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Essential services need protection from year-to-year budget swings.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Because essential services need that protection, a fixed budget cap would prevent resident votes from draining money from them. The cap would also make annual financial planning more predictable, for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Residents are more likely to participate when they can see a direct connection between their choices and local results.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: That is why direct budget votes would increase civic participation.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: One practical point is that councils can offer voting both online and in public libraries, so direct budget ballots can reach residents who cannot attend council meetings.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: But an organised minority could capture a fixed-portion budget vote; that is an objection to allowing residents to decide the spending.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: So you are saying that a limited budget vote would give residents influence without giving them control of the whole budget.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: To put Dolores's point another way, the cap would stop resident votes from taking money away from essential services.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: In other words, Dolores believes the cap would make yearly council budgeting more predictable.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: As an aside, my neighbourhood opened a new pedestrian footbridge this year.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: I have not decided how I would vote on the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Councils should allow residents to vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent. That direct control would make local spending fairer because residents would have a formal voice over money raised from their community.

utterances.speaker: Dolores

spec.topic: Should primary schools teach handwriting after students become proficient at keyboard typing?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: once children type fluently, should primary schools still teach handwriting? Siobhan, you start.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Primary schools should keep teaching handwriting, because children who take notes by hand remember lessons better.

spec.topic: Should professional basketball teams be required to disclose players’ injury details before every game?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game because pre-game injury information helps spectators understand which players are available and how the game may unfold.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A team's injury report can change opponents' preparation shortly before a game. For that reason, consistent pre-game disclosure is necessary for fair preparation by both teams.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I have attended professional basketball games in several different cities.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason for requiring disclosure is that a league-wide rule would prevent teams from gaining an advantage by withholding injury information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The rule would make competition fairer because the same information would be available to every team before the game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Mandatory injury disclosure can expose sensitive medical information and pressure injured players to return. That objection matters, but it does not outweigh the case for a carefully limited requirement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually watch televised games with a notebook nearby.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, teams should have to publish players' injury details before every game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A league-wide requirement would stop teams from selectively concealing injuries, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A clear reporting template could limit the amount of medical information that teams publish because it could balance competitive transparency with player privacy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A pre-game report can distinguish a confirmed absence from a player's uncertain status.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, pre-game injury reporting can separate confirmed absences from uncertain player statuses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The disclosure rule should allow updates when a player's condition changes after the initial report.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put that differently, the disclosure rule should permit revised reports when a player's condition changes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose a standardized injury status and any game-relevant limitation before every game. Fans need reliable information to judge whether players are likely to participate, and that need is one reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pregame injury reporting gives fans a more accurate basis for judging player availability. This is because a timely status report is more informative than rumors or last-minute speculation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The league's current injury database was launched in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Privacy is a genuine objection: requiring full diagnoses could expose private medical information about players. That objection does not defeat a narrower reporting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed requirement is a functional status report rather than a demand for a medical diagnosis. A functional status report can provide useful transparency without disclosing unnecessary medical details, which is why the limited requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Teams could manipulate vague labels such as questionable or doubtful. Since that risk would undermine the policy, independent league medical staff should audit the labels before publication; that safeguard is another reason to require the system.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The championship trophy weighs approximately twenty kilograms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Collective bargaining can define narrow privacy exceptions for the reporting rule. Because those exceptions can be written into the agreement, the policy need not ignore unusual medical circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A player's medical condition can change substantially between the morning and the game. Because of that volatility, teams should update a player's status whenever a material change occurs before tipoff.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is to say, the update duty applies whenever new information changes the player's game-relevant availability.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In practical terms, the policy would require consistent public labels rather than public treatment notes. This distinction keeps the report useful while respecting medical privacy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A written privacy exception would make the reporting rule easier for players to accept. Since player acceptance is an important condition for a workable disclosure policy, the agreement should spell out those exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, the required disclosure should identify availability and meaningful limitations while protecting private medical details.

utterances.speaker: Rania

utterances.speaker: Alina

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Routine checks can correct duplicate entries, which is why automatic registration would not create lasting duplicate entries.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Let us turn to participation. Does automatic registration affect turnout?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Many unregistered adults in a civic survey said they would vote if registration were automatic. The civic survey included four thousand respondents.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Automatic registration would make turnout data more representative, since participation would no longer depend on completing a registration form. That survey finding also supports the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Quentin

utterances.speaker: Carmen

utterances.speaker: Rania

utterances.speaker: Quentin

utterances.speaker: Beatriz

utterances.text: The central disagreement is now clear: automatic registration may broaden access while requiring safeguards against inaccurate records.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: I think knockouts in amateur boxing routinely cause serious brain injury. That danger should determine how we score bouts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Because knockouts can cause serious brain injury, amateur boxing should replace knockout victories with points-only scoring.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because that injury risk is real, points-only scoring would reduce incentives to pursue dangerous punches.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Since a knockout can seriously injure a boxer, points-only scoring would let referees stop bouts before a knockout occurs.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because knockouts can produce serious brain injury, points-only bouts would still reward technical boxing skill instead of rewarding finishing power.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Given the risk of serious brain injury from knockouts, points-only scoring would give medical staff fewer knockout emergencies to handle.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because amateur knockouts can cause serious brain injury, points-only scoring would make amateur boxing safer for young competitors.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Since knockout punches can cause serious brain injury, points-only scoring would make tournament results more consistent across venues.

utterances.speaker: Giulia

utterances.speaker: Bongani

utterances.text: Because that change would make the result depend on sustained performance, amateur boxing should replace knockout wins with points-only scoring.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Because points would accumulate throughout the bout, points-only scoring would reward fighters who perform consistently from the opening bell.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The same change would reduce the incentive for amateur boxers to chase dangerous exchanges, because points-only scoring would remove the knockout as the quickest path to victory.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

utterances.speaker: Giulia

utterances.speaker: Bongani

spec.topic: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should students have to demonstrate swimming proficiency before joining a competitive school sports team?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. Swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some coaches say that swimming has little to do with sports such as basketball or track. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams, because swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: That seems excessive to some families. They argue that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety in school sports and that a swimming requirement would unfairly exclude capable students from competitive teams.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, swimming competence is a basic safety condition for school sports. That position directly rejects the claim that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety. Put another way, schools should make swimming proficiency a condition for joining competitive sports teams; that position also rejects the claim that the requirement would unfairly exclude capable students.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I learned to swim at a community pool, but my personal experience is not the main issue.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because swimming competence is a basic safety condition, a requirement would give coaches confidence that team members can respond safely to an accidental fall into water.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Since swimming competence is a basic safety condition, the requirement would encourage students to learn a practical life skill before representing their schools.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The same safety principle is another reason for requiring swimming proficiency: it would create a common safety standard across different competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The interview is being recorded for the school newsletter. Would you apply the rule immediately?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should offer affordable swimming lessons before enforcing the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The requirement should also be humane. Since schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should allow temporary exemptions for students with medical restrictions on swimming.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Finally, because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should assess it through a basic safety test rather than competitive racing.

spec.topic: Should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Federations should impose salary caps, because caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But federations have no business setting wages, since pay is negotiated between clubs and the players' unions.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Without a cap the wealthiest clubs can outbid everyone else for every top player, which is why balance needs one. Attendance also falls when the same club wins every year, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I spent twelve years working in club academies. In capped North American leagues, ten different clubs won the title in fifteen years, which shows that caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Bernard, you are saying that under caps the titles get spread around.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But capped leagues lose their stars, because foreign clubs pay far more.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: So you are saying that salary caps send talent abroad. Incidentally, our national league introduced its cap in 2011.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, can the union objection be answered?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Caps can be set through collective agreements with the unions, so federations can impose them. Broadcasters also pay more for tight title races, which is a further reason caps work.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, the domestic league would lose its best players to other leagues, and that matters because broadcast income follows the stars.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Put another way, without a cap money alone would decide who wins. And clubs in capped leagues invest more in their youth academies, which is another reason for balance.

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.speaker: Daniela

spec.topic: Should schools let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window?

utterances.text: Schools should let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window from 8:00 to 10:00, because a common attendance window preserves shared teaching time.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But schools need one fixed starting bell for all students; otherwise teachers cannot coordinate the morning.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools need one fixed starting bell for all students.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Flexible start times would reduce late arrivals, which is a reason to adopt Esther's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The school library now has standing desks near the windows.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The school's chess club meets on Thursday afternoons.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Schools can place the first common lesson after 10:00.

utterances.speaker: Hamza

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Since schools can place the first common lesson after 10:00, teachers could preserve common lessons under the proposed attendance system.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: My conclusion is that the forum should endorse allowing students to choose their own start times within a daily attendance window. I reach that conclusion because Esther's proposal itself is workable, because the common attendance window preserves shared teaching, and because teachers can preserve common lessons.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Restorative conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences, because a court record follows a teenager into every job application.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But that ignores the victims, many of whom want a trial and a formal finding of guilt.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: On the contrary, victims who attend conferences rarely regret it, since they get answers they would never hear in court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Offenders may fake remorse to escape a trial, so conferences cannot be trusted to change behaviour.

utterances.speaker: Rashid

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The proof is that pilot schemes saw about a fifth fewer repeat offences, and the reason is that offenders must face the harm they caused.

spec.topic: Should local authorities merge neighbouring refuse-collection services to reduce administrative costs?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. Ayesha, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Merging neighbouring refuse-collection services would reduce administrative costs. The councils currently maintain separate billing, procurement, and management offices, so combining them would remove duplicated work.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I have worked on a municipal waste committee, but I am not convinced that a merger is automatically wise.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Some households put out extra garden waste after storms. That seasonal problem deserves attention even if the authorities keep their services separate.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Neighbouring councils already use compatible route-planning software. Because the software is compatible, a merged service could coordinate its depots.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Coordinated depots would reduce empty journeys by refuse vehicles. That is why the merger would also reduce administrative and operating costs.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But merging the services could make a failure at one depot disrupt collections across both councils. That risk is a serious objection to the cost-saving case.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: To put Felix's concern another way, a single depot failure could disrupt collections throughout the merged service.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Ayesha's central claim is that a merger would cut administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: An audit found that two councils saved twelve percent by jointly purchasing refuse bags and vehicle parts. That evidence supports merging the services because a larger authority could negotiate similar bulk discounts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. The administrative savings make that recommendation reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed policy is to combine neighbouring councils' refuse-collection services. Felix, you will have a final response after the break.

spec.topic: Should public schools provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Free school breakfast would prevent many pupils from beginning lessons hungry, which is a strong reason for adopting the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason is that a universal breakfast would improve pupils' readiness to learn without requiring teachers to identify children in need.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Regular breakfast provision would help pupils attend school consistently; that practical benefit also supports providing the meal to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools already have the routines needed to distribute a morning meal efficiently, so this existing capacity is another reason to establish a universal programme.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing school kitchens could serve a nutritious breakfast without major new construction, which makes universal provision a realistic public-school responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal provision would prevent children from being singled out because their families receive assistance; that protection is another reason schools should adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A well-fed pupil is more likely to benefit from the rest of the school day, and that educational payoff is a further reason for providing breakfast to every pupil.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that universal breakfast would spend public money on children whose families can already afford a morning meal, but that objection does not overturn the case for the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal provision removes the need to identify pupils by family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, universal breakfast lets every pupil eat without an income test.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the policy offers the same breakfast access to pupils from wealthy and poor households.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To say it plainly, no pupil has to declare poverty in order to receive the school meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The school orchestra rehearses on Thursday afternoons.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a blue notebook beside the keyboard.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Birgit

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Jelena

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: In other words, Rosalind supports automatically sealing minor-offence records after five crime-free years.

utterances.speaker: Birgit

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Birgit

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Birgit

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

spec.topic: Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of participants from all major demographic groups because equal demographic representation makes trial findings more applicable to the whole population.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Equal enrollment across major demographic groups is workable when trials use several recruitment sites, so that practicality is a reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I disagree with the blanket rule. Equal quotas can make a trial unfair when the eligible patient population is not evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Some major demographic groups are routinely underrepresented in clinical research. That is a strong reason to require balanced enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Soren has raised an issue about fairness, while the other guests have emphasized representativeness. Nkechi, what practical benefit would equal enrollment bring?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment gives researchers a better chance of detecting differences in treatment effects between demographic groups. That is why the requirement matters, rather than merely encouraging researchers to recruit widely.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal requires every major demographic group to have the same number of trial participants.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Soren's hospital serves a coastal region with an unusually old population.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Recruitment targets can be monitored during a trial, making equal enrollment a realistic requirement. That feasibility is another reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To sum up Nkechi's position, the central proposal is that clinical trials should enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: By equal representation, I mean giving each major demographic group the same number of places in a trial.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I have participated in three regulatory submissions.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Equal enrollment can reveal safety problems that would remain hidden in a less representative trial, which is another reason to support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed rule is a requirement for balanced demographic enrollment rather than a suggestion to recruit broadly.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: More reliable safety comparisons are another reason to require equal demographic enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays. The reason is that homework assigned during those holidays increases pressure on students who are observing religious rituals.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: But a homework ban would make it harder for teachers to keep courses on schedule. That is because major religious holidays fall on different dates.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that a holiday homework ban would disrupt course schedules.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: My family observes one major religious holiday in the spring.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Students who complete assignments before a holiday often lose time needed for family observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Moving deadlines earlier merely puts the homework workload into the week before the holiday. For that reason, moving homework is not a satisfactory solution.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, students need protected time for family observance even when homework deadlines are moved.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: The school calendar already lists major religious holidays. That resource helps teachers avoid examinations on those dates because the dates are visible in advance.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Put another way, the school calendar gives teachers advance notice of major religious holidays.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A complete homework ban would prevent teachers from assigning short revision tasks that students can do whenever convenient. That is a drawback because short revision tasks can help students retain material.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that flexible revision tasks can help students retain material.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Scheduling revision tasks after the holiday avoids interference with religious observance. That is why I could support a ban on homework during the holiday.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Because you could support that ban, the proposed compromise would protect religious observance while preserving revision.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A parent at my school prefers printed worksheets.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: That is why, in summary, schools should ban homework during major religious holidays—in other words, the original proposal stands.

utterances.text: Agnieszka, could such a scheme be administered without creating another costly bureaucracy?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The town's annual street festival is held in September.

utterances.text: The council's tax office can process the proposed discount with its existing software. Because the existing software can handle it, the administrative cost of the proposed discount would be low.

spec.topic: Should ranked-choice voting replace plurality voting in legislative elections?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference. That feature gives each ballot more information than a single mark.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice ballots record fallback preferences, counting can transfer a voter's ballot to the next preferred candidate when the first choice is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Those transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority. This is a more demanding standard than merely receiving more votes than any individual rival.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a transferred ballot still expresses a voter's preference, a candidate who reaches a majority has support from more than half of participating voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That broader support gives the winner stronger democratic legitimacy. A majority-backed winner is easier to defend to constituents who preferred another candidate initially.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices would need to revise some ballot-counting software before adopting the system. That is a practical task, not a reason to preserve a weaker voting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Plurality voting is preferable because its ballots are simpler for voters to complete. A single mark is undeniably familiar.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that simplicity does not make plurality voting preferable when ranked-choice instructions can be learned quickly. The familiar method can still produce a winner without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear ballot instructions and a worked example allow voters to learn ranked-choice voting quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because voters can understand the procedure, a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. In other words, this is the same legitimacy advantage created by majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I would want election officials to publish counting procedures before the first ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting also reduces the risk that a spoiler candidate will distort the result. A candidate's presence need not force voters to abandon their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting makes it safer for voters to rank their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because spoiler pressure is reduced, sincere voting becomes more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For these reasons, ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

spec.topic: Should emergency departments charge patients who attend for non-urgent conditions?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge people who come in with non-urgent conditions. Anders, you start.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because waiting rooms are clogged with people who could have seen a pharmacist or a family doctor. A small fee would send them to the right place.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Jin, your view?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A charge would deter poorer patients with genuinely serious symptoms from coming in, since nobody can judge for themselves whether a chest pain or a child's fever is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Staff there redirected people to other services without charging them, and it worked.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So, Jin, in other words, charging would make patients decide what counts as urgent, and they cannot do that reliably?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Many people only turn up at the emergency department because they cannot get a family doctor appointment. Attendance would fall if appointments were easier to get.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Ayesha

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.text: Organisers can require identical containers and limit handoffs to prevent personal hydration from creating an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif

spec.topic: Should teachers be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks?

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether teachers should be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks. Aurelio, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: I do. A participation grade can capture useful evidence about how students engage with learning.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Because participation grades capture engagement, teachers can notice questions and explanations that do not appear in written assignments.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Since that engagement is visible in discussion, students who explain ideas aloud can reveal misunderstandings before an exam.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Because participation is observed throughout the term, regular participation can encourage students to prepare for lessons.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: The same evidence matters for progress: because teachers see students working over time, participation records can give teachers another way to recognize improvement.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: And because engagement includes responding to classmates, a participation mark can reward collaborative listening as well as frequent speaking.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The audience has been unusually quiet during this debate. Damien, you have argued that the system needs safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes. A detailed participation rubric can make classroom contributions easier to evaluate consistently.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Because the rubric defines contribution, it can distinguish useful questions from attempts to attract attention.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since the criteria are written down, a rubric can allow teachers to record listening, teamwork and persistence.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Because students can see those criteria in advance, a rubric can tell students what kinds of contribution their teachers value.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A published rubric also helps families, because it can give parents clearer information than a vague comment about attitude.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: And because schools can compare the same categories, a rubric can make participation marks easier to moderate across different classes.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So the proposal is that teachers should be allowed to include class participation in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Exactly: teachers should be permitted to count classroom participation toward final marks.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: In other words, the debate concerns whether classroom engagement may form part of a student's final mark.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed policy would allow participation to contribute to final grades.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: To summarize, teachers would be allowed to include participation in students' final marks.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But participation grades can penalize students who are shy, anxious or still learning the classroom language. That concern makes me oppose using them in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The debate will end before the evening weather forecast. Our closing question is whether a careful rubric can answer Damien's objection.

utterances.speaker: Camille

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why legislators should not hold the pen. I should add that I chaired the commission's review panel.

utterances.speaker: Lucia

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jasper, back to the legislators.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, a legislator who draws the map is judging his own re-election prospects.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So Camille, your worry is that nobody can ever remove a commissioner from office.

utterances.speaker: Jasper

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should restaurants automatically add service charges to every bill?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill. The reason is that an automatic charge removes the diner's ability to reward good service and withhold payment for bad service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A guaranteed charge removes the incentive for staff to try hard, because staff who are paid the same whether or not diners are pleased have little reason to try.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many diners tip generously anyway, so a fixed charge adds nothing for them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Supporters say a mandatory charge makes pay fairer for kitchen and floor staff alike.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a charge that is shared out by the restaurant can be fairer than tips, which favour those who work near the customers. It is only fair, though, if the restaurant discloses how it is divided.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once worked a summer as a dishwasher in a seaside cafe.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since diners often cannot tell whether a charge goes to staff or to the owner, the practice is murky.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hidden charges breed distrust between customers and restaurants. In other words, customers feel cheated when a charge is printed in small type at the bottom of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Menu prices should simply include the full cost of labour. Put another way, honest menu prices would make service charges unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Most diners would prefer to see one honest price up front, which is why that is the right route.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The Harbour Quarter has several restaurants that already print all-in prices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants should end the practice of automatic service charges and set honest menu prices instead.

utterances.text: A personal annual training budget improves employee retention.

utterances.speaker: Adrian

utterances.speaker: Giulia

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Because a personal annual training budget improves retention, every business should give every employee one. For that same retention reason, such a budget would make employees more willing to stay with their employers.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Because tracking each employee's budget creates substantial administrative costs, a universal personal training budget would be impractical.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Since employees have different career goals, businesses should let employees choose training that matches those goals.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: But small businesses have thin profit margins, so I cannot support a rigid requirement that applies to every employer.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Hiroshi, give us your response to the concern about a one-size-fits-all rule.

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Adrian

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

spec.topic: Should pregnant patients be offered paid time off for every antenatal appointment?

utterances.text: Pregnant patients should receive paid time off for every antenatal appointment. The reason is that antenatal appointments are medically necessary rather than optional personal errands.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I disagree. A universal paid-leave rule would impose significant costs on small employers, but that concern is not the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: My sister had her first antenatal appointment on a Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Paid time off protects pregnant patients from choosing between wages and medical care, which supports offering it for every appointment.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Our office has recently replaced its staff coffee machine.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A universal entitlement would reduce pressure on pregnant patients to postpone appointments. That is another reason to offer the time off.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers can plan for recurring antenatal appointment leave because antenatal appointments are usually scheduled in advance.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Most antenatal appointments last less than two hours. That is an additional reason employers can plan for the leave.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: But predictable scheduling does not help patients whose appointments are changed at short notice.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: In other words, your point is that paid time off protects pregnant patients from having to choose between wages and medical care.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory right to paid antenatal appointment leave can be administered fairly because employers could use a standard form that records appointment dates without requiring medical details.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A second reason that the right can be administered fairly is that the rule could require reasonable notice except when an appointment is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A paid-leave entitlement would be workable with a simple employer record.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So you are saying that the entitlement could be administered with a simple employer record.

utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal would cover both routine check-ups and scans.
